lead: The first law of thermodynamics is an energy ledger. For a closed system, heat added minus work done equals the change in stored energy, and over a cycle net heat equals net work. The ledger always balances, but it does not say which of two balanced processes will actually happen, or how much of a heat supply can become work. Those gaps matter when you judge a heat engine, a refrigerator or a claim of a machine that turns all its heat into work. This chapter lists what the first law cannot decide and names the law that fills each gap.
prereq: You need the first law for a closed system and the perpetual motion machine of the first kind.

sections.h3: A balance sheet, not a compass

blocks.text: A cup of hot water left in a room cools. Heat leaves the water and enters the room. Now write the same number of kilojoules in the other direction: the room gives that heat back to the cup and the cup warms up again. Both versions satisfy Q − W = ΔU exactly. Only the first ever happens on its own. The first law cannot choose between them.

That is the first limitation: no direction. A second follows from a paddle wheel stirring water in an insulated tank. All the shaft work becomes internal energy of the water. The reverse, warm water spinning the paddle and cooling down, also balances, and never happens. Work can always turn completely into heat; heat cannot turn completely into work in a cycle. A kilojoule of work and a kilojoule of heat are equal in amount but not in usefulness, and the first law, which counts only amounts, misses the difference.
Use these five points as an exam checklist. Each is a job the first law cannot do.

items: No direction. Heat flowing from hot to cold and from cold to hot both balance energy; the first law does not say which is spontaneous.
No quality. Work and heat are both counted in kJ; the first law does not rank work above heat, or heat at 800 °C above heat at 40 °C.

It allows a perpetual motion machine of the second kind (PMM-2): a cyclic engine that takes heat from one reservoir and turns all of it into work. Q = W, so the first law is satisfied; the second law forbids it.
No criterion for equilibrium. The first law cannot say whether a process that conserves energy will occur, or where it will stop.

No difference between reversible and irreversible paths. A slow, resisted expansion and a sudden one between the same end states both satisfy Q − W = ΔU, even though their Q and W differ and the sudden one wastes the chance to do work.

blocks.text: Do not mix up the two perpetual motion machines. A PMM-1 creates energy and fails the first law; a PMM-2 conserves energy and fails the second. The first law is still necessary: any process that fails the energy balance is impossible at once. It is a filter, not the full judge.

The missing rules come from the second law of thermodynamics. Its two classical statements say that heat does not flow on its own from cold to hot, and that no cyclic engine can turn all its heat input into work (see Kelvin-Planck and Clausius statements). Entropy turns the direction into a number: the entropy of an isolated system rises in every real process and can never fall (see Principle of increase of entropy).

The second law also measures quality. Work is high-grade energy; heat is worth less the closer its temperature is to the surroundings. Available energy and exergy put a number on how much of an energy stream could become work (see Available and unavailable energy). The worked example below shows both laws applied to the cooling cup.

figure.caption: The cup of the worked example. Cooling passes 46.0 kJ from the water to the room; the reverse passes the same 46.0 kJ back, so the first law accepts both. Only cooling raises the total entropy of cup and room (by 0.0127 kJ/K), so only cooling happens.

spec.aria: Two panels. Left, solid border: heat of 46.0 kJ flows from a cup of water at 80 °C to a room at 25 °C; the first law balances and total entropy rises by 0.0127 kJ/K, allowed. Right, dashed border: the same 46.0 kJ flows back from the room into the cup; the first law still balances but total entropy would fall by 0.0127 kJ/K, forbidden.

examples.question: A cup holds 0.2 kg of water at 80 °C in a room at 25 °C. Take c = 4.18 kJ/kg·K for water. (a) Find the heat the water loses as it cools to room temperature. (b) Show that the reverse process also satisfies the first law, and use the entropy change of the cup and the room to show which direction is possible.
steps: Q = mcΔT = 0.2 × 4.18 × 55 = 0.836 × 55 = 45.98 kJ, about 46.0 kJ, which the water rejects to the room.
Reverse: the room gives 46.0 kJ to the water and it warms from 25 °C back to 80 °C. The energy balance closes with the same 46.0 kJ, so the first law allows both directions.
Entropy change of the water as it cools: ΔS<sub>cup</sub> = mc ln(T₂/T₁) = 0.836 × ln(298.15/353.15) = 0.836 × (−0.1693) = −0.1415 kJ/K.
The room is so large that its temperature stays 298.15 K: ΔS<sub>room</sub> = Q/T = 45.98/298.15 = +0.1542 kJ/K.
Total: ΔS = −0.1415 + 0.1542 = +0.0127 kJ/K > 0, so cooling is possible. The reverse would give −0.0127 kJ/K, a fall in the entropy of the isolated cup-and-room system, which the second law forbids.
examples.answer: The water loses 46.0 kJ. Both directions balance energy, but only cooling raises the total entropy (by 0.0127 kJ/K), so only cooling happens.

traps: Saying a cold cup warming on its own would break the first law. Its energy balance is perfect; it breaks the second law.
Calling a PMM-2 a first-law violator. A PMM-2 satisfies the first law and fails the second; a PMM-1 fails the first.
Writing “heat can never become work”. Heat cannot become work completely in a cycle; a single process such as an isothermal expansion can turn all the heat it takes in into work.
Treating a kilojoule of work and a kilojoule of heat as equally useful. The first law counts both; the second law ranks them.

quiz.q: State any three limitations of the first law of thermodynamics.
quiz.a: Any three of: it gives no direction for a process; it does not rank the quality of heat and work; it allows a PMM-2; it gives no criterion for equilibrium; it does not separate reversible from irreversible processes.

quiz.q: Define a perpetual motion machine of the second kind.
quiz.a: A cyclic device that takes heat from a single reservoir and turns all of it into work, with no heat rejected; it satisfies the first law and breaks the second.

quiz.q: Why does the first law allow a cold cup in a warm room to warm up on its own, though it never happens?
quiz.a: The same kilojoules can be written as flowing from the room to the cup, and the energy balance still closes. Direction is not part of the first law; it is set by the second.

quiz.q: Why are a kilojoule of work and a kilojoule of heat not equal in quality?
quiz.a: Work can turn completely into heat, for example by friction or a paddle wheel. In a cycle heat cannot turn completely into work; some must be rejected. So work is the higher-grade form.

quiz.q: 0.5 kg of water cools from 90 °C to 30 °C (c = 4.18 kJ/kg·K). Find the heat rejected.
quiz.a: ΔT = 60 K, so Q = 0.5 × 4.18 × 60 = 125.4 kJ is rejected.

quiz.q: An inventor claims a cyclic engine takes 100 kJ of heat from one reservoir and delivers 100 kJ of work. Check it against both laws.
quiz.a: First law: Q<sub>net</sub> = W<sub>net</sub> = 100 kJ, so it passes. It rejects no heat, so it is a PMM-2; the second law forbids a cyclic engine with 100 percent efficiency.

quiz.q: A slow, resisted expansion and a sudden expansion of the same gas have the same end states. What does the first law fail to tell you about them?
quiz.a: Both satisfy Q − W = ΔU with the same ΔU, but the first law cannot say which is reversible, how much work the sudden one lost, or how much entropy it created; the second law and exergy analysis answer that.

beyond: In plant design, exergy analysis ranks the losses that an energy balance hides: a boiler can pass on 90 percent of its fuel energy and still destroy much of its work potential by heating water across a large temperature gap. Pinch analysis uses the same second-law idea to cut fuel use in process plants. Search next for “second law efficiency”, “exergy destruction” and “pinch analysis”.
